title: Tail-latency decomposition and fanout tradeoffs - design notes
content:
Meeting: Tail-latency decomposition + fanout tradeoffs (arch sync)
Date: 2025-01-15
Facilitator: Morgan Li
Attendees: Morgan Li, Priya Kapoor, Ethan Ruiz, Samir Nair, Jules Park, Anika Gomez (observability)
Duration: 60m
Location: Zoom / runtime-arch sync

Purpose:
- Align on sources of tail latency in the serving runtime and practical mitigations that preserve cost SLOs.
- Decide on a small set of design changes we can prototype in Q1 to reduce 99.9th/99.99th latency without regressing throughput.

Agenda:
1) Quick recap of SLOs and customer pain (Priya)
2) Decomposition of observed tail (Ethan + Anika)
3) Fanout and routing alternatives (Samir)
4) Tradeoffs matrix and opt-in plan (group)
5) Action items + owners

Recap / context:
- Customer-facing SLO target: 95% < 150ms, 99% < 450ms, 99.9% < 1.2s for short-seq generation workloads (configurable per deployment). Several customers reported intermittent spikes at p99.9 with multi-second tails during moderate load.
- Current runtime uses per-request routing to the freshest compatible variant, dynamic batching, and KV cache warm/cold behavior that impacts the first few tokens of some sessions.

Observed tail sources (decomposition):
- Cold KV cache misses for conversation-heavy requests -> per-request spike at first token (~100-700ms variance).
- Oversized batching when sequence-length distribution skews (batch assemble latency) -> occasional head-of-queue waits (~50-400ms).
- Model hotloading / variant switch during rollout or auto-scale event -> transient 200ms-1.5s pauses observed in internal traces.
- GPU scheduling preemption or cross-tenant interference (more common on Dedicated lower-tier pools) -> long tails up to multiple seconds in worst cases.
- Network serialization and large context assembly in the routing proxy (edge) -> 30-200ms.

Design alternatives considered:
A) Proactive KV prewarming: maintain lightweight predictive warmers keyed by recent conversation ids. Pros: reduces KV miss tails. Cons: complexity, extra memory I/O, potential stale kv risk.
B) Tail-aware batching policy: small fast-path batch queue + long-assembly slow queue; set a hard max assembly wait per batch. Pros: reduces head-of-queue waits. Cons: reduces batching efficiency -> higher token cost.
C) Async fanout with speculative partial responses: send to primary low-latency variant and speculative to a fallback heavier variant in parallel; accept first complete response. Pros: reduces visible tail; graceful quality fallback. Cons: increased compute cost and more complex token accounting.
D) Localized model pinning during rollouts: prevent variant switch for warm sessions; perform gradual migration windows. Pros: fewer hotload pauses. Cons: slower rollouts, coordination overhead.
E) Priority queueing + preemptible tasks: short requests get higher scheduling priority; long-running/low-priority jobs can be preempted. Pros: aligns latency vs throughput. Cons: fairness implications, implementation complexity with stateful kv sessions.

Tradeoffs and group discussion highlights:
- We want low-friction mitigations first (low-risk, measurable win): Tail-aware batching (B) + Localized pinning (D) are highest ROI with relatively modest infra changes.
- Proactive KV prewarming (A) looked promising but is risky in Private deployments where KMS/HSM constraints and network limits may make proactive reads expensive. We should prototype a conservative warmer limited to hosted and dedicated where we can control IO.
- Async fanout/speculation (C) gives the best latency curve but doubles compute cost for a subset of calls. We should gate this behind a config flag and cost-meter it (Redwood Optimize integration) before wider rollout.
- Priority queueing (E) requires scheduler changes and careful SLO/fairness mapping; tabled for Q2 spike reduction plan.

Decisions made (consensus):
1) Implement a two-path batching micropolicy: fast-path with smaller max-assembly-wait (e.g., 10ms) for requests with short expected seq length; slow-path retains larger batching windows for bulk throughput. This will be opt-in per model route initially.
2) Add session-level variant pinning during rollouts for sessions with warm kv/cache state. Rollout controller will mark sessions as "pinned" for a configurable TTL (default 5 minutes).
3) Prototype a conservative KV prewarmer for hosted/dedicated only; implement warm-only on high-traffic conversation routes (top-10 routes by qps). Private deployments will be excluded by default.

Telemetry and metrics to add (Observability work):
- New trace tags: batch_path=fast|slow, session_pinned=true|false, kv_warm=true|false, variant_load_trigger=hotload|rollout|scale.
- 99.9/99.99 percentiles by route and path; also compute p99.9 delta pre/post fast-path.
- Cost meter for speculative fanout (if prototyped): compute time and tokens consumed per request and per successful fast-path win.
- Alerting: p99.9 regression >20% for 15m -> paging to runtime-oncall.

Prototype plan / milestones (Q1):
- Week 1-2: design doc + API for batch_path hints + session pin TTL (owner: Samir).
- Week 3-4: implement fast-path batching queue and feature flag; internal e2e test harness (owner: Ethan).
- Week 5: deploy to staging, synthetic load tests with skewed seq distributions. Capture baselines. (owner: Priya + Anika for telemetry)
- Week 6: staged rollout to hosted beta routes; measure p99/p99.9 and throughput changes. Decide on further rollout. (owner: Morgan)
- Parallel: lightweight KV prewarmer prototype limited to top-10 routes in a canary pool (owner: Samir).

Open questions / risks:
- How do we surface the extra cost of speculation to customers? Need billing design for speculative CPU/GPU usage (link to billing RFC).
- Session pin TTL tradeoff: too long pins slow rollouts; too short pins don’t reduce hotloads. Default 5m was chosen heuristically; need A/B.
- Private deployments may have IO constraints; prewarmer disabled by default but we need clear docs and an opt-in pattern.
- Scheduling fairness: fast-path may starve slower analytical/embedding workloads on shared Dedicated pools. Need scheduler quota checks.

Action items (owner, ETA):
- Samir: write the small design doc for session pinning + prewarmer scope (2025-01-22).
- Ethan: implement fast-path batching prototype + unit tests (2025-02-05).
- Priya: add telemetry spans and dashboard skeleton; prepare attack scenarios for staging (2025-02-05).
- Morgan: coordinate hosted canary rollout and measure p99.9 changes; produce brief report with cost delta (2025-02-19).
- Anika: define experiment and metrics for KV warmer effectiveness (2025-02-05).

Notes to self / loose ideas for future follow-ups:
- Consider ML-driven prewarmer that reads only high-entropy context keys (avoid full kv reads).
- Explore integration with Redwood Optimize to recommend fast-path vs slow-path per route based on cost/latency curves.
- Investigate kernel-level scheduling knobs for pinned sessions to reduce hotload pauses during model swap.

References mentioned in the meeting:
- RDW-4123 (customer p99.9 incidents)
- github.com/redwood-inference/inference-runner/pull/987 (early batching prototype)
